Pierre de Fermat. A French lawyer and mathematician from sixteen hundred seven to sixteen sixty-five whose work in number theory, calculus, and probability was revolutionary, yet he published almost nothing in his lifetime. His famous conjecture—Fermat's Last Theorem—remained unproven for three hundred fifty-eight years until Andrew Wiles solved it in nineteen ninety-five.

Fermat's Last Theorem states that no three positive integers a, b, and c satisfy a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n for any integer n greater than two. While this is true for n equals two—Pythagorean triples exist—it is false for all larger values of n. This conjecture remained unproven for three hundred fifty-eight years, becoming the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics, until Andrew Wiles solved it in nineteen ninety-five using modern techniques.

Fermat's Little Theorem asserts that if p is prime and a is not divisible by p, then a to the power p minus one is congruent to one modulo p. This is foundational to modular arithmetic and modern cryptography, used in encryption and secure communications today. He also proved that every prime of the form four k plus one can be uniquely expressed as the sum of two squares.

Independently, he developed analytic geometry alongside Descartes, using coordinates to represent curves algebraically. His method of adequality anticipated calculus—he treated infinitesimals as quasi-zero quantities to find tangent lines and extrema. He applied calculus informally to maxima and minima problems decades before Newton and Leibniz formalised the field.

In correspondence with Pascal, Fermat founded modern probability theory by solving the problem of points: how to divide the stakes fairly in an interrupted game. His probabilistic reasoning laid the groundwork for expected value and the foundations of statistics.

Fermat was a gentleman mathematician who published little, leading to priority disputes and the loss of many proofs. Yet his influence was enormous. His scribbled notes in margins of classical texts sparked centuries of research. In the margin of a book, he famously wrote of his Last Theorem: "I have a truly marvellous proof of this, which this margin is too narrow to contain." This note became the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics, captivating mathematicians for three hundred fifty-eight years. When Wiles finally proved it, his proof required modern machinery—elliptic curves and the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture—that would have amazed Fermat himself.
